messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Radiologist
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Vignette:
Marianne had been 76 for only a few months when she finally agreed to speak to a therapist, though the need for help had been building for much longer. A retired radiologist, she had spent most of her life in ordered, well-lit rooms where images could be studied, measured, and named. That older confidence did not survive the years she spent as a civilian in a war zone, when daily life became organized around sudden danger and the body’s reflexive searching for where it might come from. She described one episode in particular as the point after which ordinary life never quite felt ordinary again: she was outside, trying to move quickly between buildings, when she realized that people were approaching in a way that left her no clear way to judge whether they were safe. The uncertainty itself felt intolerable. After that, she said, she learned to watch every face, every hand movement, every pause in a stranger’s stride. Even now, in a suburban grocery store or at the entrance to her own apartment building, she finds herself tracking the people around her before she can hear what they are saying, bracing whenever someone comes toward her in what others would consider a normal, harmless way.

In the months and years that followed, Marianne’s world narrowed. She began avoiding unfamiliar places because she felt she could not assess the danger there, and she found herself declining outings that would once have seemed routine. Her husband noticed that she stopped making future plans, even the small ones that used to give shape to their days. If he suggested a trip, a dinner with friends, or even a simple appointment booked too far ahead, she would become uneasy and put it off. She said planning felt like tempting a fate she could not control. Instead, she spent long hours on her phone, scrolling through games and internet pages until the day blurred into the next. She did not describe this as enjoyment so much as escape; it was one of the few ways she could keep her mind from circling back to what happened. She also tried to avoid anything that might stir strong feelings of any kind, not only fear but even pleasure or tenderness, because emotional intensity itself felt risky to her, as if once opened she might not be able to close it again.

What remained most troubling to her was the way the memory itself resisted being held. When she tried deliberately to remember the war-time event, she found it difficult to access in a clear sequence, as though the scene were behind frosted glass. She could recall fragments — a street, the sense of being cornered by uncertainty, the faces of strangers approaching — but she could not easily put the frightening event into words. In session, she would sometimes go quiet and look away, then say that language felt too small or too blunt for what had happened. She also spoke of a painful shame that rose whenever the memory surfaced. It was not a diffuse embarrassment but an intense, bodily self-reproach, as if remembering meant being back in the same moral atmosphere of helplessness and exposure. That shame made her withdraw further into silence, especially from her husband, who wanted to understand but often found only a changed expression and a request to be left alone.

At home, Marianne’s day was shaped by vigilance. She constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger, even in places that had once felt familiar and safe. When she sat near a window or walked through a parking lot, her attention moved automatically to doorways, vehicles, and the distance between herself and other people. The ordinary approach of a stranger could make her tense immediately, and she would step aside or leave before a conversation could begin. These habits had made her smaller in her own life. She missed family gatherings more often, avoided errands in unfamiliar parts of town, and found herself increasingly dependent on predictable routines. Her husband had come to do more of the practical navigating, while Marianne quietly organized her hours around the avoidance of distress.

She sought help when she noticed how complete the narrowing had become. The screen, the silence, and the refusal to make plans could no longer fully keep the memories and the sense of threat at bay. What frightened her most was not only the memory itself, but the possibility that she might spend the rest of her life braced against danger, unable to trust strangers, places, or even her own mind. What she hoped for was modest but deeply felt: to be able to move through ordinary days without constant alarm, and to remember the past without feeling that shame and fear were still waiting to catch up with her.
